newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Legras warns of grain surplus build-up.
newsitem.headline: Legras warns of grain surplus build-up.

text.p: European Union grain intervention stocks are expected to surge to 58 million tonnes by the end of 2005/06, Guy Legras, the European Commission's Director General for Agriculture, said on Wednesday.
Legras, presenting long term prospects for the grain, milk and meat markets, said that cereals yields were expected to continue to grow at a steady rate and outstrip growth in domestic demand.
The projections assume no change in EU farm policy, respect of GATT trade commitments and maintenance of a 17.5 percent reference rate for cereals and oilseeds set-aside.
"The projections do not prejudge the real set-aside rate. It's a very conservative forecast. Set-aside could be much lower," Legras told a news briefing.

At Tuesday's Farm Council in Luxembourg, Farm Commissioner briefed ministers on the projections by Commission's agriculture department, which support his bid to convince reluctant member states to accept further reforms.
The compulsory set-aside rate for the 1997 harvest is five percent and France, supported by several other member states, this week called for a zero rate next year.
Legras explained that the 17.5 percent reference rate was used because that was the rate in the EU set-aside regulation.
Grain intervention stocks were only expected to rise slightly this season, he added.

Stocks are forecast rising to 5.2 million tonnes at the end of 1996/97 (July/June), from 2.7 million tonnes at the end of 1995/96. Stocks stood at 33 million tonnes when the Common Agricultural Policy was reformed in 1992.
The EU was able to offload a large part of the stocks by subsidising exports onto the world market.
Domestic demand for animal feed rose by 12 million tonnes a year after guaranteed prices were reduced as part of the reform.
Legras cautioned that the EU will no longer be able to export unlimited quantities of subsidised grain due to limits set under the 1994 GATT agreement.
But he noted OECD, FAO and USDA reports projecting increasing world demand, notably in Asia, and firm world prices.
"Over the next eight years market trends are very positive," Legras said.
The EU would be able to export without subsidies when world prices climbed above EU levels but this would not happen regularly, he said.
"It happened last year and could happen again but can't be considered as a normal situation," he said.
Beef stocks are expected to rise to 1.5 million tonnes in 2005/06, from 18,000 tonnes, despite EU measures to cut output after the mad cow crisis.
But dairy stocks, apart from skimmed milk powder, are not expected to cause concern.
